findings_qualitative.value: The SiO emission traces a highly collimated, symmetric bipolar jet spine, while CS emission traces lower-velocity gas near the protostar and only reaches high velocities further downstream where SiO declines.

evidence.quote: The emission shows clear chemical and kinematic differentiation: SiO traces the high-velocity jet spine, while CS is observed at lower velocities close to the protostar, and only reaches high velocities at larger distances.

findings_qualitative.value: Position-velocity diagrams show a continuous triangular velocity structure with a velocity spread at the base of the flow, consistent with a steady magneto-centrifugal disk wind launched over a range of radii rather than an X-wind or wide-angle entrained flow.

evidence.loc: Position-velocity diagrams, terminal velocities and episodic emission
evidence.quote: Importantly, and consistently within the first moment maps in Figures 3 and 4, the base of the flow exhibits a clear velocity spread rather than a single narrow high-velocity spike.

evidence.loc: Position-velocity diagrams, terminal velocities and episodic emission
evidence.quote: The PV structure with its layered velocity distribution close to the source and moderate inclination-corrected terminal speeds of $\sim$80 km s$^{-1}$, is therefore most consistent with a magneto-centrifugal disk wind.

findings_qualitative.value: Vertical emission stripes in the PV diagrams and periodic temperature enhancements (>60 K) spaced by ~0.2 arcsec (~540 au, ~32 yr) indicate quasi-periodic modulation of the wind likely originating from disk processes at ~9 au.

evidence.quote: Especially evident in the blue-shifted lobe (top-right of the figure) are temperature enhancements in the SiO gas periodically on these intervals, with gas temperatures reaching an excess of 60K.

evidence.loc: Implications for Jet Launching and Disk–Jet Coupling
evidence.quote: We favour an interpretation in which the observed knots in the wind launched from within 1 au arise from some form of modulation process or structure further out in the disk (at the $\sim9$ au radius).

findings_qualitative.value: Well-ordered, narrowly collimated, disk-driven jets can be launched and maintained even within dense, clustered high-mass star-forming regions.

evidence.quote: This demonstrates that well-ordered, narrowly collimated, disk-driven jets can be launched and maintained even in the dense, competitive environments characteristic of high-mass star formation.

claims.hypothesis: The SMA3 jet is driven by a steady magneto-centrifugal disk wind launched over a range of disk radii rather than an X-wind or wide-angle entrainment-driven outflow.
claims.experiment: Analyze the spatial morphology, moment 0 and 1 maps, and position-velocity (PV) diagrams of SiO (J=5-4 and 6-5) emission along the jet axis.
claims.result: The jet has a collimation ratio of 4.75, de-projected velocity of ~80 km s^-1, and a two-sided triangular PV morphology with a broad velocity spread at the base and layered velocity stratification (lower velocities along the edges, highest velocities along the central axis).
claims.finding: The SMA3 jet is powered by a steady magneto-centrifugal disk wind launched from radii of order 0.5-1 au rather than an X-wind or wide-angle entrained flow.

evidence.loc: Position-velocity diagrams, terminal velocities and episodic emission
evidence.quote: This morphology matches the expected PV signature of a disk wind launched over a range of radii, rather than an X-wind confined to a narrow launching annulus.

evidence.loc: Position-velocity diagrams, terminal velocities and episodic emission
evidence.quote: The PV structure with its layered velocity distribution close to the source and moderate inclination-corrected terminal speeds of $\sim$80 km s$^{-1}$, is therefore most consistent with a magneto-centrifugal disk wind.

claims.hypothesis: Shock processing along the SMA3 jet produces chemical and kinematic stratification between grain-sputtering tracers (SiO) and denser post-shock/entrained gas tracers (CS).
claims.experiment: Compare moment 0 and moment 1 maps and spectra of SiO (J=5-4, 6-5) and CS (J=5-4) across the SMA3 outflow.
claims.result: SiO traces the high-velocity (+-60 km s^-1 LOS) jet spine over ~5800 au (age ~343 yr) with little emission at V_LSR, whereas CS peaks at V_LSR near the core and shows high-velocity (+-50 km s^-1 LOS) knots further out at ~7270 au (age ~520 yr) after SiO intensity declines.
claims.finding: The jet is chemically and kinematically stratified: SiO forms promptly in fast grain-processing shocks along the spine, while CS traces cooler, denser post-shock and entrained gas further downstream.

evidence.quote: The emission shows clear chemical and kinematic differentiation: SiO traces the high-velocity jet spine, while CS is observed at lower velocities close to the protostar, and only reaches high velocities at larger distances.

evidence.loc: Chemical Stratification: The Relationship Between SiO and CS Emission
evidence.quote: This offset is consistent with expectations for chemically layered shocks: SiO is produced promptly in high-velocity, grain-processing regions, while CS forms or survives preferentially in the denser, cooler post-shock gas.

claims.hypothesis: Periodic emission peaks and temperature enhancements along the jet trace quasi-periodic modulation of the wind from the protostellar disk.
claims.experiment: Measure spacing of vertical emission stripes in SiO PV diagrams and compare with pixel-by-pixel LTE excitation temperature maps derived from the SiO (6-5)/(5-4) ratio.
claims.result: Emission peaks and temperature enhancements (>60 K vs mean 42 K) recur at ~0.2 arcsec intervals, corresponding to a de-projected separation of ~540 au and an ejection timescale of ~32 yr, which matches a Keplerian orbital timescale at ~9 au around a 0.7 M_sun protostar.
claims.finding: While the 80 km s^-1 jet is launched within <1 au, its mass-loading or ejection is quasi-periodically modulated on a ~32 yr timescale by disk processes or substructures at ~9 au.

evidence.quote: The periodic spacing of $\sim0.2''$ corresponds to a de-projected knot separation of $\sim540$ au and an ejection timescale of $\sim32$ yr, when using the derived jet velocity of 80 km s$^{-1}$.

evidence.loc: Implications for Jet Launching and Disk–Jet Coupling
evidence.quote: We favour an interpretation in which the observed knots in the wind launched from within 1 au arise from some form of modulation process or structure further out in the disk (at the $\sim9$ au radius).

claims.hypothesis: Compact, well-ordered, disk-driven jets can form and persist without disruption inside dense, clustered high-mass star-forming regions.
claims.experiment: Measure the symmetry, collimation, dynamical age, and energetics (mass, momentum, energy) of the SMA3 jet embedded within the S255N massive star-forming clump.
claims.result: The red and blue lobes have nearly identical masses (~2.18x10^-3 and 2.13x10^-3 M_sun), column densities, and mass flow rates (0.6x10^-5 M_sun/yr), maintaining a collimation ratio of 4.75 and linear axis over ~343-520 yr.
claims.finding: Even within a clustered high-mass star-forming environment, a protostar can launch and maintain a highly symmetric, collimated, and dynamically coherent disk-driven jet similar to those in isolated low-mass protostars.

evidence.quote: Despite forming within a clustered high-mass star-forming region, the jet exhibits a high degree of symmetry, collimation, and dynamical coherence more commonly associated with protostars forming in isolation or less crowded star-forming regions.

This provides valuable evidence that compact, disk-anchored jets can arise even within dense and turbulent environments where multiplicity, feedback, and radiative heating could otherwise disrupt the collimation process (cite: Frank2014; Qiu2011; Seifried2012; Peters2014).

why_this_data.value: High angular resolution (<0.1 arcsec) Band 6 ALMA observations in two configurations (C-4 and C-7) resolve the compact SMA3 continuum core and two rotational transitions of SiO (5-4 and 6-5) plus CS (5-4) to probe shock excitation, morphology, and kinematics.

evidence.quote: This paper presents new ALMA Band 6 observations of SMA3, providing sub-arcsecond resolution imaging of the sub-mm continuum, SiO, and CS emission.

why_this_method.value: Using the mean of the continuum-axis inclination (lower limit) and jet opening angle (upper limit) brackets the true system inclination; per-channel column density integration provides more accurate momentum and kinetic energy estimates than integrated line profiles.

evidence.loc: Opening and inclination angles and their implications for velocities and jet age
evidence.quote: We explore both options below and use their mean value for further analysis, since the former defines a lower limit and the latter an upper limit on the true inclination angle.
This per-channel method allows for more detailed momentum calculations.

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: X-wind jet launching model: rejected because PV diagrams show a broad velocity spread at the base of the flow rather than a single narrow high-velocity spike from a narrow launching annulus.

evidence.loc: Position-velocity diagrams, terminal velocities and episodic emission
evidence.quote: Importantly, and consistently within the first moment maps in Figures 3 and 4, the base of the flow exhibits a clear velocity spread rather than a single narrow high-velocity spike. This morphology matches the expected PV signature of a disk wind launched over a range of radii, rather than an X-wind confined to a narrow launching annulus.

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Quarter-power contour for jet opening angle measurement (as in Offner et al. 2011 and Dunham et al. 2024): replaced with half-power contour due to signal-to-noise ratio considerations.

evidence.loc: Opening and inclination angles and their implications for velocities and jet age
evidence.quote: This method is similar to that used in (cite: Offner2011) and (cite: Dunham2024), however they instead used the ‘quarter power’ contour for their analysis because of better signal to noise ratios in their moment maps.

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Rotational signature analysis in dense core tracers (CS, CH3CN): not pursued because jet velocities dominate the kinematics and rotational signals cannot be distinguished.

evidence.quote: It could be expected that these higher density tracers might show rotational signatures in the protostellar core or potentially even a protostellar disk, however their dynamics are dominated by the jet velocities, and any rotational signal cannot be distinguished from their emission profiles.

limitations_admitted.value: The 260 GHz spectral window did not have SiO 6-5 at its centre, so the highest blue-shifted emission from SiO 6-5 was not captured in the bandpass.

evidence.quote: We note that the 260 GHz spectral window was not setup with SiO 6-5 in its centre, and the highest blue-shifted emission from that line is not captured in our bandpass.

limitations_admitted.value: The continuum emission may trace a geometrically thick protostellar envelope rather than a thin disk, making the disk-derived inclination angle only a lower limit.

evidence.quote: However, since this is expected to be a very young region, it is unclear whether this assumption is valid, and we could instead be seeing a geometrically thick protostellar envelope.

limitations_admitted.value: The flow-derived opening angle (54.5 deg) was measured by eye and lacks formal uncertainties.

evidence.loc: Opening and inclination angles and their implications for velocities and jet age
evidence.quote: We only have formal uncertainties on the ‘disk’ derived inclination angle, since the ‘flow’ derived value was measured by eye.

limitations_admitted.value: Internal shocks may decelerate the overall flow velocity, affecting kinematic age estimates.

evidence.loc: Opening and inclination angles and their implications for velocities and jet age
evidence.quote: we calculate an outflow length of 7270$\pm$2160 au and derive a kinematic age of 520$\pm$270 yr for the high velocity CS emission, with the caveat that any internal shocks may be decreasing the overall flow velocity.

limitations_admitted.value: High excitation temperatures (>200 K) and large uncertainties on the northern edge of the jet near the target required excluding that region when computing the mean excitation temperature.

evidence.quote: Near the target, on the northern edge of the jet, the derived temperature is quite high (in excess of 200 K), as is the uncertainty on the estimate in that region.

referee_caveats_inferred: The dust opacity value kappa_nu at 250 GHz used to compute the 0.007 M_sun dust mass (and 0.7 M_sun total mass) is never stated in the text.

The SiO J=6-5 (0.10 x 0.07 arcsec) and J=5-4 (0.11 x 0.08 arcsec) maps have slightly different synthesized beams and position angles (40.87 deg vs 135.25 deg), and it is not explicitly stated whether the cubes were smoothed to a common resolution before the pixel-by-pixel excitation temperature ratio was computed (though radio_beam's common_beam method is mentioned).

Slight internal numerical inconsistencies in the text: the plane-of-sky SiO lobe length is stated as 2.15 arcsec in Section 3.2.1 but 1.65 arcsec in Section 5, and the terminal velocity is stated as ~80 km/s throughout but ~74 km/s at the end of Section 4.2.

Assuming optically thin SiO emission and a fixed SiO/H2 abundance of 10^-7 introduces substantial systematic uncertainty in the outflow mass, momentum, and energy that dwarfs the small formal statistical uncertainties reported in Table 3.
